intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, give you something to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, test yourself with the questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: The Measurement Problem
sections.big_idea: You cannot see what you most want to measure, so every score is **a model's estimate** built from visible answers.
in_plain_words: Reading ability, empowerment and food insecurity cannot be observed. What you collect are answers: right or wrong, agree or disagree, yes or no. A measurement model is the bridge from those answers back to the hidden trait, and its assumptions can be checked.

The usual shortcut is the sum score, which treats every item and every gap as equal. It orders people reliably but does not say how far apart they are. IRT lets items differ and places people and items on **one common scale**, at the price of needing more data.

nodes.label: Responses
nodes.sub: right or wrong, yes or no

diagram.caption: four stages from the unseen trait to a number

key_terms.meaning: A hidden characteristic inferred from answers, written θ.
The bridge linking the unseen trait to the seen responses.
A count of right answers; ordinal at best.
Classical Test Theory, which works on the total score.
Item Response Theory, which models each item and person.

worked_example.title: Why 6 of 12 hides information
worked_example.setup: Two children each get 6 of 12 items right. Child A passed the six easiest items. Child B passed six hard items and missed easy ones.
steps: A sum score gives both children the same number, 6.
Check which items each passed. A passed the easy half, a pattern consistent with item difficulty.
B's pattern is unusual: passing hard items while missing easy ones is improbable under the model.
IRT reads the pattern and places the children at different positions, or flags B's pattern for checking.
worked_example.answer: The same total can hide different patterns. IRT uses the pattern and the sum score cannot.

mistakes: Treating a reported score as a direct measurement. Every score is a model output, including a simple total.
Fixing a badly written item set with a better estimation method. Errors in the first two stages cannot be repaired in the fourth.
Averaging sum scores and reading the difference as a gain, forgetting that the scale is ordinal at best.
Using IRT on a tiny sample. With about 80 respondents a well-built sum score is the better tool.

recall.q: What does 'latent' mean in latent trait?
recall.a: The trait is inferred from responses under a model and never observed directly.

recall.q: Name two things a sum score assumes that often fail.
recall.a: Every item is worth the same, and every gap between scores is the same size.

recall.q: Which response format points towards Rasch or 1PL?
recall.a: Yes/no experience items with no guessing route, such as food insecurity items.

recall.q: When might you reasonably skip IRT?
recall.a: When none of comparability, fairness, shorter forms, targeted precision or honest error is something your programme needs.

recall.q: What is the honest trade-off between CTT and IRT?
recall.a: IRT tells you more but needs substantial data; CTT needs only modest data.

sections.title: Classical Test Theory & Its Limits
sections.big_idea: CTT is simple and everywhere, but its statistics depend on **the sample, the form and a single error figure** for everyone.
in_plain_words: CTT writes an observed score as a true score plus random error. Reliability, in its four versions, says how much of the variation is signal. Cronbach's alpha is the workhorse, but it rises with item count and says nothing about what is measured.

Three limits push practitioners towards IRT. Item p-values change with the group that sat the item. Person scores change with the form. And one standard error is quoted for everyone although the test is **far more precise in the middle** than at the ends.

diagram.caption: three limits, each with an IRT answer

key_terms.meaning: Expected score over infinite retests, tied to one test.
Share of score variance that is true score, 0 to 1.
Internal-consistency estimate; rises with item count.
Proportion who got an item right, the CTT difficulty.
Standard error of measurement, one figure in CTT.

worked_example.title: One item, three schools
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures from the deck: item Q is answered correctly by 88% of a high-ability school, 61% of a mixed government school and 34% of a struggling school.
steps: Each p-value gives CTT's verdict: easy, moderate and hard.
The item itself did not change between the schools.
The spread between the extremes is 88 − 34 = 54 percentage points.
That whole spread comes from who sat the item, so the p-value mixes item and people.
worked_example.answer: One item produced a 54-point spread in p-values, which is a property of the samples and no property of the item.

mistakes: Reading alpha above 0.9 as proof the scale is unidimensional. Alpha rises with item count.
Celebrating an alpha above about 0.95. It usually signals near-duplicate items and wasted respondent time.
Carrying CTT item statistics from a pilot to the field or pooling them across studies.
Using one SEM to report confidence in a child far below grade level, where the interval is too narrow.

recall.q: Write the basic CTT equation.
recall.a: Observed score = True score + Error, or X = T + E.

recall.q: Why can a scale have good alpha and still be unstable?
recall.a: Alpha measures internal consistency; test-retest reliability asks a separate question.

recall.q: What is the CTT difficulty statistic?
recall.a: The p-value, the proportion who got the item right.

recall.q: Where does a test measure most precisely?
recall.a: Near the middle of the ability range, where many items sit close to a person's level.

recall.q: What condition belongs on every IRT answer to a CTT problem?
recall.a: If the model fits.

sections.title: The Big Idea of IRT
sections.big_idea: Put people and items on **one shared ruler**, then model the chance of a correct answer as an S-shaped curve.
in_plain_words: IRT places each person's trait (θ) and each item's difficulty on one continuum. A person above an item will probably succeed; below it, probably fail. The model gives a probability and never a promise, and every theta comes with a standard error.

The probability follows a rising S-curve that never dips. By convention theta is centred on zero in a reference group, so zero is no proficiency standard. The nice properties, such as sample-free items, are **conditional on the model fitting**, which Section 9 tests.

left.title: CTT
items: Score and p-value differ in kind
Cannot ask who is above which item
Statistics depend on sample and form

right.title: IRT
items: Theta and b share one scale
Properties travel if the model fits

key_terms.meaning: A person's position on the latent trait scale.
Trait scale centred near zero, about −3 to +3.
Probability of a correct or endorsing response at θ.
More trait never lowers the chance of success.
Putting separate calibrations onto one scale.

worked_example.title: Is she above or below the item?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative values on the shared scale: a child sits at θ = 0.5, an easy item at b = 0 and a hard item at b = 1.
steps: Compare the child with the easy item: 0.5 − 0 = 0.5, so she sits above it by half a unit.
Compare her with the hard item: 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, so she sits below it by half a unit.
Above an item means success is likely; below it means success is unlikely.
The model gives a probability, so neither outcome is certain.
worked_example.answer: She is likely to succeed on the easy item and unlikely on the hard one, but IRT promises neither.

mistakes: Treating theta = 0 as a standard of proficiency. It is the reference-group average at calibration.
Reading a probability of 0.7 as a prediction that this child will get the item right.
Reporting a theta without its standard error.
Comparing thetas from two separate calibrations without linking them first.

recall.q: What is the central move of IRT?
recall.a: Placing each person's trait and each item's difficulty on one shared continuum.

recall.q: What shape is the probability curve, and what must it never do?
recall.a: An S-shaped logistic curve that rises with theta and never dips.

recall.q: Why is a negative theta not necessarily failure?
recall.a: Zero is the average of the calibration reference group, so negative can mean below that group's average.

recall.q: How does b read on an endorsement scale?
recall.a: As severity: how much of the condition it takes to endorse the item.

recall.q: What is the endorsement-scale analogue of guessing?
recall.a: Social desirability.

sections.title: The Item Characteristic Curve
sections.big_idea: The ICC is **one picture** from which you read difficulty, discrimination and guessing, and spot a broken item.
in_plain_words: The ICC plots probability of success (y) against theta (x), one curve per item. Where it crosses 0.5 gives b, the slope there gives a, and the lower asymptote gives c. A fourth parameter for careless errors exists but is rarely estimated.

Read it in three moves: pick a theta, go up to the curve, read across. A valid curve only rises. A dip signals a mis-keyed, ambiguous or unrecoded item. Scoring then finds the theta that **best fits a person's whole pattern**, so the same raw score can mean different things.

levels.label: Lower tail
levels.sub: P near 0 or c, little information

diagram.caption: the three landmarks of an ICC

key_terms.meaning: Curve of probability of success against theta.
Steepest point, where the item sorts people best.
Always rising: more trait, higher chance.
Estimating item parameters from a large sample.
Statistics flagging improbable response patterns.

worked_example.title: Diagnose a downward curve
worked_example.setup: Item 9 on an attitude scale shows a clean downward ICC and negative discrimination.
steps: Do not conclude anything about the item yet.
Check the answer key and the item wording for ambiguity or a trick.
Check the coding script: was a reverse-worded item recoded?
Fix any error and refit the model.
Only if the curve still dips is it a finding about the item.
worked_example.answer: Most downward curves come from coding errors, so fix and refit before interpreting.

mistakes: Reading the logistic formula as a discovery. It is a convenient modelling choice and the normal ogive looks almost identical.
Trusting a fitted curve without plotting the empirical proportions correct over it.
Using maximum likelihood scores without knowing that all-right and all-wrong patterns have no finite estimate.
Assuming two children with 6 of 12 sit at the same theta.

recall.q: What three things do you read from the 50% crossing, the slope and the floor?
recall.a: Difficulty b, discrimination a and guessing c.

recall.q: Where is an item's information at its maximum?
recall.a: At the inflection, the steepest point of the curve.

recall.q: Name two causes of a non-monotonic curve.
recall.a: Any two of: mis-keyed item, ambiguous wording, trick or double-barrelled item, reverse-coded and not recoded.

recall.q: What do the scoring steps produce?
recall.a: A theta with a standard error, which is the person's IRT score.

recall.q: Why can adding easy items for strong children change almost nothing?
recall.a: Easy items carry near-zero information at high theta.

sections.title: Item Difficulty: the b Parameter
sections.big_idea: b places an item on the trait scale: **higher b means a harder item**, and it shares units with theta.
in_plain_words: Difficulty b is the theta where success probability is 50% under 1PL or 2PL. Because it shares units with theta, you can compare a person with an item directly and choose items whose b values surround the people you need to measure.

On attitude scales b reads as severity. It is estimated from data and absorbs wording, translation and layout, so never assign it by intuition. An item map shows **blind spots**, the gaps along the scale where the test measures poorly.

diagram.caption: illustrative reading ladder, easiest to hardest

key_terms.meaning: Theta at which success probability is 50%.
How much of a condition it takes to endorse an item.
Chart of where items sit along the theta scale.
A gap on the map where the test measures poorly.
Choosing items near the people you must measure.

worked_example.title: Which ladder items help?
worked_example.setup: Use the illustrative ladder: letter at −2.0, word at −0.8, sentence at 0.2, paragraph at 1.0, comprehension at 1.8. A group sits near θ = 1.
steps: Items far below the group are very likely correct and give little information.
The letter item is 1 − (−2) = 3 units below the group, so it is wasted.
The paragraph item has b = 1.0, so 1.0 − 1.0 = 0, right on the group's level, and gives high information.
The comprehension item sits above the group and is informative for its stronger members.
worked_example.answer: For a group near θ = 1, the paragraph and comprehension items help most and the letter item is wasted.

mistakes: Assuming higher b means easier because higher CTT p-values mean easier. Higher b is harder.
Believing a question that looks advanced must be hard. Difficulty comes from how people actually respond.
Reusing b estimated in one language for a translation. The translated item is a different item until shown otherwise.
Building a test whose items bunch together and leave gaps on the item map.

recall.q: What does b = 0 mean for the item?
recall.a: Moderate difficulty: a person at theta 0 has a 50% chance.

recall.q: Under a 3PL model, where is b?
recall.a: Where probability is halfway between c and 1, which is above 0.5.

recall.q: How should b be read on a food-insecurity scale?
recall.a: As severity.

recall.q: Why does a wide-range assessment need items spread across the range?
recall.a: Otherwise it measures one grade well and the others poorly.

recall.q: How do you set b?
recall.a: Estimate it from data and sanity-check surprises, never assign it by intuition.

sections.title: Item Discrimination: the a Parameter
sections.big_idea: a is the **slope of the curve at its midpoint**: how sharply an item separates people just below and just above its b.
in_plain_words: A steep item changes the chance of success a lot for a small move in theta, so it is a sharp ruler near its b. Away from b even a steep item is flat. Information rises with the square of a, which is why selection routines love steep items and why they can bunch them together.

A flat item may be ambiguous, off-topic or simply placed where nobody sits. A negative a means stronger people do worse and is usually a keying or coding error. Difficulty and discrimination vary independently, so **describe a bank with a scatter of a against b**.

left.title: Steep item (high a)
items: Leaps from low to high quickly
Useful only in a narrow band

right.title: Flat item (low a)
items: Similar odds across a wide range

key_terms.meaning: Steepness of the ICC at its midpoint.
An item with very low a that adds almost nothing.
The logistic 1.7, applied differently by software.
Items bundled on one passage.
A pool of calibrated items.

worked_example.title: Square the slope
worked_example.setup: The deck says information rises with the square of a. Compare an illustrative flat item with a = 1 and a steep item with a = 2, both at the same difficulty and measured at b.
steps: Flat item: a × a = 1 × 1 = 1 unit of relative information.
Steep item: a × a = 2 × 2 = 4 units of relative information.
The steep item carries 4 ÷ 1 = 4 times as much.
worked_example.answer: Doubling a quadruples the relative information at b, which is why selection favours steep items.

mistakes: Dropping a flat item before plotting it. Nobody near its b can look the same as a poor item.
Leaving a negative a in the bank. Treat it as a data problem first and fix the key or coding.
Letting an automated routine pick only steep items at one difficulty.
Comparing a values with a published table without checking the 1.7 constant.

recall.q: What does higher a mean?
recall.a: A steeper ICC and a sharper separation of people near the item's b.

recall.q: Why is a steep item narrow?
recall.a: It is informative only near its own b and flat elsewhere.

recall.q: What usually causes negative discrimination?
recall.a: Keying errors or reverse-worded items that were not recoded.

recall.q: What plot should you draw to review a bank?
recall.a: A scatter of a against b, one point per item.

recall.q: Which agency items tend to have low a?
recall.a: Broad, socially desirable statements such as participating in household decisions.

sections.title: Guessing & the Model Family
sections.big_idea: Each model adds one parameter and one data requirement: **start simple and add only what the data supports**.
in_plain_words: On multiple choice nobody scores zero, so the curve has a floor called c. Ignoring it makes items look easier and inflates low-end scores, which understates the learning gap. True/false puts the floor near 0.5; open response and yes/no experience items need no c.

The model family runs from Rasch (b only) through 2PL (a and b) to 3PL (a, b and c). More parameters always fit the sample better, but the question is whether they replicate. **Let fit and theory decide**, with sample size close behind.

diagram.caption: each step adds realism and demands more data

key_terms.meaning: Lower asymptote of the ICC, the guessing floor.
Items differ in difficulty only.
Items differ in difficulty and discrimination.
Adds a guessing floor to the 2PL.
Raw score maps directly to theta under Rasch.

worked_example.title: Fix c from the format
worked_example.setup: A multiple-choice test uses 4-option items in one section and true/false items in another. You decide to fix c at 1 divided by the number of options.
steps: For the 4-option items: 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.
For the true/false items: 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.
Estimated c often comes out lower than these because weak respondents can eliminate an option.
State that c was fixed, which is more honest than reporting an unstable estimate.
worked_example.answer: Fix c at 0.25 for 4-option items and 0.5 for true/false items.

mistakes: Fitting a model with no guessing parameter to multiple-choice data and trusting low-end scores.
Using the 3PL on a yes/no scale, where guessing does not arise.
Choosing the fanciest model instead of the one the sample can support.
Fitting Rasch by deleting every misfitting item and never checking whether the deletions were the informative ones.

recall.q: What chance floor does a four-option item have?
recall.a: About 0.25.

recall.q: What does ignoring guessing do to b?
recall.a: Biases it downward, so items look easier than they are.

recall.q: What does Rasch fix to be equal across items?
recall.a: The discrimination a.

recall.q: When is the 2PL needed?
recall.a: When item quality plainly varies and you have the sample size.

recall.q: What is the diagnostic plot for unmodelled guessing?
recall.a: The lower-tail plot, where observed proportions sit above the modelled curve at low theta.

sections.title: Information & Precision
sections.big_idea: Information is **precision at each point on the scale**, and standard error is 1 over its square root.
in_plain_words: Each item informs most near its own b, more so as a rises. Test information is simply the sum of item information, so you can design a test by choosing items. Standard error at any theta is 1 divided by the square root of information, which means error is smallest where information peaks.

This replaces one blanket reliability figure with a curve. Place the information where the decision is made: near a cut-score for pass/fail, evenly for a population description. Because people and items share a scale, an adaptive test can pick each next item for **maximum information** at the current estimate.

diagram.note: more information means less error, and both vary along theta

key_terms.meaning: How much an item reduces uncertainty about theta.
Sum of item information functions.
1 divided by the square root of information.
The theta where a classification decision is made.
Items chosen to be most informative at the current theta.

worked_example.title: From information to error
worked_example.setup: Illustrative test information at a certain theta is 16. At another theta, in the sparse tail, it is 4.
steps: Take the square root of 16, which is 4.
SE at the first theta: 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.
Take the square root of 4, which is 2.
SE at the tail theta: 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.
worked_example.answer: Four times less information doubles the error: 0.25 at the peak against 0.5 in the tail.

mistakes: Reporting a single reliability figure for a test whose precision varies along the scale.
Assembling an instrument by topic coverage when the decision falls at one cut-score.
Classifying a child as below grade level without giving the standard error.
Assuming an adaptive test needs only an algorithm. The item bank is the usual barrier.

recall.q: What is the formula for standard error in terms of information?
recall.a: SE = 1 divided by the square root of information.

recall.q: How is test information built from items?
recall.a: It is the sum of the item information functions.

recall.q: Where should information be concentrated for a pass/fail decision?
recall.a: Near the cut-score.

recall.q: Why does CTT's single SEM mislead at the extremes?
recall.a: It understates the error there and overstates it in the middle.

recall.q: What does an adaptive test do after each answer?
recall.a: Updates theta and picks the most informative unused item near it.

sections.title: Validating Scales & DIF
sections.big_idea: Validation is what **entitles you to the claims** of Sections 3 to 8: fit, one dimension, local independence and no DIF.
in_plain_words: Sample-free items and comparable scores hold only if the model fits. Check fit with statistics and, above all, with plots of the empirical curve over the modelled one. Check unidimensionality with factor analysis and a content review, and local independence by looking for shared passages, chained items and duplicates.

DIF asks whether two people at the same theta, from different groups, have different odds on an item. It is different from a group gap in theta, since it conditions on theta. DIF **flags an item for review**, and the review decides whether the cause is irrelevant to the construct.

diagram.caption: four checks, each tied to a promise

key_terms.meaning: One latent trait accounts for the responses.
Given theta, items give no clues about each other.
Several items on one passage, usually dependent.
Different odds at the same theta across groups.
The curve shifts; non-uniform DIF changes its slope.

worked_example.title: DIF or a real gap?
worked_example.setup: Classify four observations using the deck's rule that DIF conditions on theta.
steps: Girls score higher overall. That is a group difference in theta, so no DIF.
Girls at the same theta do better on item 7. Same trait, different odds, so DIF.
One region scores lower overall. That alone is a trait difference, so no DIF.
One region at the same theta fails item 12 more often. That is DIF, so send the item for content review.
worked_example.answer: Items 7 and 12 show DIF; the two overall gaps do not.

mistakes: Reading a significant item-fit statistic as meaningful with 5,000 respondents. Nearly every item will misfit.
Treating DIF as proof of unfairness. It flags an item for review.
Explaining away a real group gap as item bias, or dismissing real bias as a gap.
Dropping flagged items without recording the decision.

recall.q: What does DIF condition on?
recall.a: Theta: it compares people with the same trait level.

recall.q: Give a typical source of local dependence.
recall.a: Several questions on one reading passage, a testlet.

recall.q: Why is the empirical-versus-modelled plot better than a p-value alone?
recall.a: Fit statistics depend on sample size, while the plot shows the size and location of the departure.

recall.q: What should you do about a DIF item caused by a poor translation?
recall.a: Retranslate and back-translate.

recall.q: Is all DIF bias?
recall.a: No, a topic taught in one state and not another may be legitimate and should be documented.

sections.title: Applications in Development
sections.big_idea: IRT's payoff in practice is **a fixed ruler**: comparable scores across forms, years and groups, if anchored and screened.
in_plain_words: Large assessments such as NAS and ASER, cross-national studies and programme endlines use IRT to place children on one scale. Equating links different forms through shared anchor items, so a rise in scores reflects learning and no change in the test. Anchor drift is the practical hazard.

The same logic runs through FIES, empowerment scales, asset indices and attitude screeners. Each has its own difficulty: severity order, response shift, asset lists that are local. Payoffs such as shorter forms and fairer measures hold **only for the groups you screened**.

diagram.caption: rotate the items, keep the ruler

key_terms.meaning: Putting forms on a common theta scale.
Items shared across forms to link them.
An anchor's difficulty changing between years.
Eight-item food insecurity scale, basis of SDG 2.1.2.
A programme changing what people consider normal.

worked_example.title: How many anchors?
worked_example.setup: The deck's rule of thumb: anchors should be at least 20% of the test or 20 items, whichever is larger. Illustrative: a form has 60 items.
steps: Work out 20% of the test: 60 × 0.2 = 12.
Compare with the floor of 20 items.
Take whichever is larger.
The anchor set must also span the difficulty range.

mistakes: Equating on anchors that have become familiar or leaked, so their difficulty drifts.
Using too few anchors, or anchors clustered in difficulty.
Reading a rise in empowerment scores as programme impact without considering response shift.
Deciding DIF groups after data collection, or screening groups too small to analyse.

recall.q: What does equating do?
recall.a: Places different test forms onto a common theta scale, usually through anchor items.

recall.q: Why does a repeated survey need to check anchors?
recall.a: An item may become familiar or leak and get easier, shifting the scale.

recall.q: How many items does FIES have, and what response type?
recall.a: Eight yes/no experience items.

recall.q: Is the DHS wealth index built with IRT?
recall.a: No, it uses principal components.

recall.q: Who benefits from DIF screening?
recall.a: Only the groups you actually screened.

sections.title: Assumptions, Limits & Tools
sections.big_idea: IRT is powerful and **conditional**: check the assumptions, fit the simplest defensible model, and translate theta for people.
in_plain_words: The five assumptions are one trait, local independence, the right model, monotonicity and no DIF. Break one and the guarantees stop holding without warning. IRT is data hungry, too: roughly 200 respondents for Rasch, 500 for 2PL and 1,000 for 3PL, with spread of ability mattering as much as the count.

Follow a sensible workflow: check dimensionality, fit the simplest model, examine items, screen DIF, then revise and score. Report a standard error, give proficiency bands in plain language and remember that **a precise number can still measure the wrong thing**. Tools such as mirt, ltm and TAM do the fitting.

key_terms.meaning: One trait, local independence, right model, monotonicity, no DIF.
A judgement process for placing cut-points on theta.
R package for most uni- and multidimensional IRT models.
Plain-language label for a range of theta.
How software reports a and b, including the 1.7 constant.

worked_example.title: Pick the model
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's situation table for three projects.
steps: A yes/no experience scale with 300 respondents suits Rasch.
An ability test with varied item quality and 800 respondents suits 2PL.
A high-stakes multiple-choice test with 2,000 or more respondents can justify 3PL.
A scale with several distinct traits needs a multidimensional model or separate scales.
worked_example.answer: Rasch, 2PL, 3PL, and separate or multidimensional models respectively.

mistakes: Saying 'the model did not fit' and stopping, without finding which assumption failed.
Mixing parameters from two packages without converting for the 1.7 constant or intercept form.
Scoring with items you would drop, so thetas change as the bank is revised.
Presenting a cut-score as if the data derived it. Standard setting is a judgement.

recall.q: Name the five assumptions.
recall.a: Unidimensionality, local independence, correct model, monotonicity, no DIF.

recall.q: Roughly how many respondents does a 2PL need?
recall.a: About 500 or more.

recall.q: What is the first step of the workflow?
recall.a: Check dimensionality and local independence.

recall.q: How should you report a theta of 1.2 to a programme officer?
recall.a: In plain language, such as 'can read a short paragraph with comprehension', with the standard error.

recall.q: Which kind of validity can IRT not supply?
recall.a: Whether the scale measures the concept, such as empowerment, which depends on content validity.

notes.2: Use the agenda as your map. Sections 1 to 3 build the idea, sections 4 to 8 teach you to read one curve and its three parameters, and sections 9 to 11 cover validation and practice. If time is short, read **section 4 first**, then return to section 2.
notes.4: Reading ability, empowerment and hunger cannot be seen. Only answers can. That gap is why every score you report is **a model output**. Look at the table and ask, for each row, what else the observed answers might be measuring. A total score hides this question; IRT states it.
notes.5: Learn the four stages as a chain: trait, items, responses, inference. A flaw early in the chain cannot be mended by clever statistics late in it. Before you fit anything, **check the items and the dimensionality**, because the estimation step is the easy part.
notes.6: Match each setting to its response type before you choose a model. Pass/fail tasks suggest Rasch or 2PL, yes/no experiences suggest Rasch, and multiple choice with guessing suggests 3PL. **The response format drives the choice.** Ordered categories use extensions of the same logic.
notes.7: A sum score treats every item and every gap as equal. Two children can both score 6 of 12 and have passed quite different items. Remember the last row: a total is **ordinal at best**, so averages and differences of it, especially for change over time, stand on shaky ground.
notes.8: Hold this comparison in your head for the whole course: CTT works on the test, IRT works on each item. The last row is the honest trade-off. With around 80 respondents, **a well-built sum score beats an IRT model** that cannot estimate its parameters.
notes.9: Ask which of these five benefits your programme needs: comparability, fairness, shorter forms, accuracy at a decision point, honest error. Each justifies the extra work. **If you need none of them, you probably do not need IRT**, and that is a perfectly good answer.
notes.10: This roadmap splits the course into foundations and use. Foundations cover difficulty, discrimination and guessing; use covers information, validation and applications. Read it with section 3 in mind, because every later section is a detail on **one S-shaped curve**.
notes.12: Read X = T + E as the whole of CTT. Your score is a true score plus random error, and the job is to shrink the error. The true score belongs to **this particular test**, so it is no ability that exists apart from the instrument. Systematic error stays invisible.
notes.13: Reliability is the share of score variation that reflects real differences between people. The four methods answer four different questions, so they can disagree. A scale can hang together internally and still **wobble over time**, which alpha alone will never reveal.
notes.14: Treat alpha as a summary and never as a certificate. It climbs when you add items, whatever those items measure. A value above about 0.95 is usually **a warning of near-duplicate items**, so read the wording before you celebrate. Use the four misreadings as a checklist.
notes.15: Here is the first limit. The p-value is just the share who got an item right, so it moves with the sample. Same item, same wording, different group, different difficulty. **The item did not change; the people did.** CTT item statistics therefore cannot be pooled across studies.
notes.16: Work from the numbers: 88%, 61% and 34% are one physical item sat by three schools, and CTT calls it easy, moderate and hard. The figures are illustrative, but the lesson is real: **a p-value mixes the item with the people who answered it**.
notes.17: Now the mirror image. A person's CTT score depends on the form they sat, so an easier paper lifts it. Two children of equal ability can differ by form alone. Comparison across schools or years becomes **guesswork** until the forms are properly linked.
notes.18: CTT quotes one standard error for everyone, yet a test measures the middle best. Top scorers find every item easy and very weak children find every item hard, so both are measured poorly. A single SEM gives intervals **too wide in the middle and too narrow at the ends**.
notes.19: This slide is the bridge to IRT. Each CTT problem has an IRT answer in the right column, and every answer carries an unspoken condition: **if the model fits**. Without fit you get sample-dependent parameters with more decimal places. Section 9 is where that condition gets tested.
notes.21: Picture one ruler with people and items both marked on it. A person above an item will probably get it right; below it, probably not. CTT cannot do this, because score and p-value are **different quantities in different units**. Everything else in the course follows from this one move.
notes.22: Theta usually runs from about −3 to +3, centred on zero for the reference group. Zero is a convention and carries no standard of proficiency. A negative theta may simply mean **below the average of the calibration sample**, so be careful showing raw theta to non-specialists.
notes.23: IRT gives probabilities. A probability of 0.7 promises nothing about this child, and a theta of 1.2 is an estimate with error. Read the right-hand column as a list of **over-readings to avoid**, and always ask for the standard error that goes with a theta.
notes.24: Learn the shape: near 0 far below the item, 0.5 at b, near 1 far above. The curve only ever rises, and that monotonicity is the assumption that matters. The logistic formula itself is a convenience, since the normal ogive looks almost identical.
notes.25: Look at this chart before you read on. At θ = 0 the chance is 50%, and it climbs toward certainty as theta rises. Cover the caption and **describe the curve in your own words**: where it starts, where it steepens, where it levels off.
notes.26: Three gains, each with a condition. Item properties travel across samples, person scores across tests, and everything shares a metric. The table lists when each holds and when it fails. Invariance is also **only up to a linear transformation**, so separate calibrations must be linked.
notes.27: The same S-curve serves attitudes and experiences, with b read as severity. 'Worried about food' sits low; 'went a whole day without eating' sits high. In place of guessing, watch for **social desirability**, which shifts by interviewer, setting and group.
notes.28: Treat this as your table of contents for the next sections. Each row is one property of the same S-curve. Notice the last row: validation and DIF decide whether you are **entitled to claim** anything above it. Sections 1 to 8 describe; section 9 earns.
notes.30: Learn the ICC as three readings of one picture: the 50% crossing gives b, the slope there gives a, and the floor gives c. The fourth parameter, a ceiling, is rarely used. In most development work **b and a carry the substance**, and c appears only when guessing is possible.
notes.31: Practise the three moves with a pencil: pick a theta, go up to the curve, read across. The table doubles as an item-review checklist. A flat curve across your whole range means a wasted item, and **a downward slope means a mis-keyed one**.
notes.32: Name the landmarks: lower tail, inflection, upper tail. Information peaks at the inflection and fades in both tails. That is why adding easy items for strong children changes almost nothing, since those items carry **near-zero information at that theta**.
notes.33: Use this single clean curve as your reference picture. It is monotonic, S-shaped and runs from 0 to 1. Whenever you meet a messy empirical curve later, **lay it beside this one** and note exactly where it departs.
notes.34: A fitted curve that dips is a symptom, so run the four checks in the table before blaming the item. The commonest cause is a reverse-worded item that was never recoded, which gives a clean downward curve. **Fix the coding and refit** before drawing any conclusion.
notes.35: Reading several ICCs together is how bank reviewers work. Horizontal position gives difficulty and steepness gives discrimination. Try it on the four curves in the chart: **say which is easiest and which sorts best** before you read the caption.
notes.36: Scoring finds the theta that makes a person's whole answer pattern most likely. Know your estimator. Maximum likelihood fails for anyone with all items right or all wrong, and Bayesian estimators repair that by **shrinking toward the mean**. Report the standard error with the score.
notes.37: Two children can both score 6 of 12 and sit at different thetas, depending on which items they passed. A child who passes hard items and misses easy ones gives an improbable pattern. **That flag is information CTT throws away**, and person-fit statistics formalise it.
notes.39: Higher b means harder, which feels backwards if you grew up on p-values. Memorise the ladder from −2 (very easy) to +2 (very hard). Remember too that under a 3PL, b sits where probability is halfway between c and 1, which is **above 0.5**.
notes.40: Read the 50% line across the three curves. The easy item crosses at −1, the middle one at 0 and the hard one at +1. Steepness is the same and position differs. **Harder items slide to the right**, and that crossing point is b.
notes.41: Because b and theta share units, you can compare a person with an item directly. A child at 0.5 is above the easy item and below the hard one. Use this for targeting: pick items whose b values **surround the people you most need to measure**.
notes.42: Work down the ladder from letter to comprehension. The b values are illustrative, and the ordering is what an ASER-style tool captures. Then use the second table: for a sample near −1.5, **the paragraph items are wasted**. Spread items across every grade you test.
notes.43: On attitude and experience scales, read b as severity. Worry sits low and going a whole day without eating sits highest. A good scale **spreads mild to severe items**, so it can place households all along the continuum. A severity order that fails to replicate deserves investigation.
notes.44: Gaps on an item map are blind spots. Here the test thins out between b = −0.8 and 0.2, so children in that band are measured less well. Draw a map like this for your own instrument and **fill the gaps you find**.
notes.45: Never assign b by intuition. It comes from responses and absorbs wording, translation, layout and order. A translated item is, empirically, a different item until shown otherwise. Treat any surprising b as **a prompt to inspect the item**.
notes.47: Higher a means a steeper curve and a sharper split between people just below and just above b. Use the band table as a rough guide: below 0.5 contributes little, above 2.0 is excellent but narrow. Check **your software's scaling constant** before comparing with published values.
notes.48: Compare the two curves. Both cross 50% at θ = 0, yet the steep one leaps from low to high across a narrow band and the flat one barely separates anyone. **Same b, very different usefulness.**
notes.49: A steep item is a sharp ruler, but only near its own b. Information grows with the square of a, so steep items win any automatic selection. Watch for the trap: left alone, a routine will **stack steep items at one difficulty**.
notes.50: A flat item gives similar odds to everyone. Before dropping it, run through the four checks in the table. Low a can simply mean nobody in the sample sits near its b, which is a sampling problem. **Plot the empirical curve first.**
notes.51: A downward curve means stronger people do worse, which should never happen. Treat it as a data problem until proven otherwise: mis-keying, a reverse-worded item not recoded, or a shifted column. If it survives all four checks, **it is telling you something real** about the construct.
notes.52: Remember the pairing: b says where the item works and a says how well it works there. They vary independently, so describe a bank with a scatter of a against b. Gaps along the b axis are coverage gaps, and **points near the bottom are dead weight**.
notes.53: On an empowerment scale, a good item separates more from less empowered women near its severity. Broad, socially desirable statements such as 'participates in household decisions' attract near-universal agreement, so they carry little. Prefer **specific, recent, behavioural items**.
notes.54: Steeper is not always better. A test of only very steep items measures one region superbly and the rest poorly. Decide the purpose first: one pass/fail cut-score favours concentration, while describing a population needs steep items **spread across the range**.
notes.56: On four-option multiple choice, a child who knows nothing still gets about one in four right, so the curve flattens at a floor called c. True/false puts the floor near 0.5. Open response and yes/no experience items need no c. **Match the model to the format.**
notes.57: Compare the two curves in the chart. The amber one never drops below about 0.25, because a very low-ability child still has a one-in-four chance. Find the floor first, and **then read b and a above it**.
notes.58: If you ignore guessing, the floor is misread as an easier item. Difficulty is biased downward and low-end scores are inflated, so children who know very little look as if they know something. That **understates the learning gap**. Check whether observed proportions sit above the model in the lower tail.
notes.59: Each model adds one parameter and one data requirement: 1PL estimates b, 2PL adds a, 3PL adds c. More parameters always fit the calibration sample better, so the real test is whether they **replicate in a new sample**.
notes.60: Rasch fixes a equal across items, giving parallel curves, simple scoring and stability on modest samples. The price is the equal-discrimination assumption. Know your camp: Rasch users treat the model as a standard the data must meet, while 2PL users **fit the model to the data**.
notes.61: Free a and the curves can cross. Use 2PL when item quality plainly varies and you have several hundred respondents. The practical test is to fit both. If the a values cluster, Rasch was fine; if they run from 0.4 to 2.5, **forcing equality distorts the scale**.
notes.62: The 3PL adds c and demands the most data, since c lives in the sparse low tail. With modest samples, fix c at one over the number of options. Skip it altogether for **yes/no scales**, where guessing does not arise.
notes.63: Start simple and add parameters only when the data demands and supports them. Work the situation table: 300 respondents on a yes/no scale gets Rasch, 800 on a varied test gets 2PL, 2,000 or more on a high-stakes test gets 3PL. The last row shows that **two scales** can beat one bigger model.
notes.65: Information is precision at each point on the scale. An item informs most near its own b, and more as a rises. Because information adds across items, you can design a test by choosing items, and **one excellent item can outweigh several mediocre ones**.
notes.66: The chart shows one item's information peaking at θ = 0, its b. Read it as a spotlight: people near the item are lit well and people far away sit in the dark. **Locate your respondents relative to the peak** before trusting the item.
notes.67: Add the item curves and you get the test information function. Where items pile up the test measures precisely; where they thin out it measures poorly. The three-item example here is broad and peaks near 0. **Build your own picture by stacking curves.**
notes.68: Hold the one formula of this section: standard error equals 1 divided by the square root of information. High information gives small error and low information gives large error. The SEM curve is the **mirror image** of the information curve.
notes.69: Set the two columns side by side. CTT reports one error for everyone; IRT lets it rise in the tails and fall in the middle. If your decision sits at an extreme, as when finding children far below grade level, **report the standard error with every score**.
notes.70: Choosing items by their b is how you aim a form. The chart moves the information peak right by centring items near +1.5. Use this for grading top performers or pinpointing a cut-score. Two forms of the same length can be **excellent for some children and poor for others**.
notes.71: Put information where the decision is made. A pass/fail call needs items near the cut, two cuts need two peaks, and a population description needs an even spread. Instruments are usually assembled by topic coverage, so **say which you chose** whenever coverage and targeting conflict.
notes.72: In adaptive testing the computer picks each next item to be most informative at the current theta, updates, and repeats until the standard error is small enough. It reaches the same precision in far fewer items. The real bottleneck is **the calibrated item bank**, a multi-year investment.
notes.74: List what you must check: model fit, one dimension, local independence and no DIF. Each IRT promise leans on one of them, as the table shows. Plan for it early, because in a real development cycle **validation takes longer than writing the items**.
notes.75: Use fit statistics, but trust the picture. Chi-square item fit flags almost everything with 5,000 respondents and almost nothing with 200. **Plot the empirical curve over the modelled one** and judge the size and location of the gap.
notes.76: Unidimensionality means one theta explains the responses. It never holds exactly, so ask whether the departure is large enough to distort scores. Use factor analysis and a content review. A child strong in vocabulary and weak in reasoning receives a theta that **blends the two**.
notes.77: Local independence fails when items lean on one another, as with five questions on one passage (a testlet). The result is **inflated reliability**, because dependent items get counted as independent evidence. Bundle such items together or rewrite them.
notes.78: DIF compares two people at the same theta from different groups. Same trait, different odds, so the item is reading something else for one group. Uniform DIF shifts the curve and non-uniform DIF changes its slope. Remember that DIF **flags an item for content review** and says nothing about intent.
notes.79: In the chart one item has two curves. At any given theta, Group B has lower odds, so the item is effectively harder for them at the same trait level. That is **uniform DIF**: the same shape, shifted apart.
notes.80: Keep DIF and group gaps apart. If girls score higher overall, that is a trait difference. DIF appears only when girls and boys at the same theta differ on one item. **Conditioning on theta is the whole trick**, and mixing the two misreads the output.
notes.81: When an item shows DIF, investigate before deleting. Check the content for unfamiliar contexts, check the translation, then revise or remove. Some DIF is legitimate, such as a topic one state teaches and another does not. **Document every decision**, including items you keep.
notes.83: IRT lets 'reading at grade-2 level' mean the same on form A and form B. NAS, ASER and cross-national studies use it to compare across grades, states and years. Cross-national work stretches the assumptions most, so look for the **DIF and invariance analyses** those studies publish.
notes.84: Equating stitches separate forms into one scale. Shared anchor items are the usual design because nobody has to sit two tests. Quality depends on the anchor set, which should span the difficulty range and number at least 20% of the test or 20 items, **whichever is larger**.
notes.85: Without equating, a rise in scores might just be an easier form. Equating holds the ruler fixed while items rotate. The hazard is anchor drift, where a familiar or leaked item gets easier. **Check anchor stability first** and drop drifted anchors from the link.
notes.86: FIES has eight yes/no experience items modelled with Rasch and linked to a global reference scale, and it underpins SDG indicator 2.1.2. Note each design choice and its reason in the table. This is **quiet infrastructure**: a global indicator resting on a measurement model.
notes.87: Empowerment scales must show that mobility, decisions and assets form one trait, that severity order holds across settings, and that DIF is absent across caste, region and religion. The last row describes response shift: a programme can change what counts as normal. **Say so openly** in any evaluation.
notes.88: Asset indices place households on a wealth continuum from patterns of ownership. A motorcycle and a mud floor sit at different points, just like easy and hard items. Remember the DHS index uses principal components and no IRT, and both approaches **depend on the asset list** chosen.
notes.89: Knowledge, stigma and quality-of-life scales use the same logic. Grade knowledge items to match the campaign level, order stigma statements by how much prejudice endorsing them takes, and concentrate screener information at the clinical cut-point. Prefer an **established validated scale** when one exists.
notes.90: Four payoffs: shorter instruments, comparable numbers, fairer measures, targeted precision. The table keeps each one honest. Fairness holds only for the groups you screened, so **choose your DIF groups at design** and make sure the sample can support them.
notes.92: Memorise the five assumptions and what breaks with each. Violations give no warning, so 'the model did not fit' is no diagnosis; find which assumption failed. The last row matters most in development work, where **we mostly compare groups**.
notes.93: Use these sample sizes as rough anchors: about 200 for Rasch, 500 for 2PL, 1,000 for 3PL. They are illustrative. Spread matters as much as count, since a thousand respondents at one theta cannot calibrate a wide bank. With a small sample, consider **fixing parameters from a published calibration**.
notes.94: IRT cannot rescue badly written items, and a neat theta can hide a contested concept. It can show that items form a coherent scale and cannot show that the scale measures empowerment. That question belongs to content validity and to the people concerned. **Precision and validity are separate achievements.**
notes.95: Pick the tool by the job: mirt for most models, ltm as a gentle start, TAM or eRm for Rasch and large-scale work, difR or lordif for DIF, Stata or commercial packages for institutional work. Whatever you use, **check the parameterisation** it reports, including the 1.7 constant.
notes.96: Follow the five steps in order: dimensionality, simplest model, item fit, DIF, then revise and score. Calibrate and validate first, so reported thetas do not change under you. Keep **the item parameters versioned with the sample**, since a theta needs the parameter set that produced it.
notes.97: Translate theta into language people act on: 'can read a short paragraph', or '12% more children reached the paragraph level'. Always give the standard error. Standard setting for cut-points is **a judgement, and should be documented as one**.
notes.98: Choose one general text and one applied report and read them together. Embretson and Reise is the readable start. The FIES documentation is public and the best available worked example of building an experience-based scale. The deck also pairs with Data Literacy, Survey Design and M&E 101.
notes.99: Use this slide as a self-test. For each takeaway, try the check in the right column without looking back. If you keep only one, keep the last: **the guarantees hold only if the assumptions do**. Without validation, an honest sum score with a stated caveat is the better instrument.
